facts.statement: means a lack of order or an untidy, confused state
facts.source_detail: Merriam-Webster defines the noun as a lack of order and Cambridge describes the state as untidy or unorganized.

facts.statement: can mean a breach of public peace or social order
facts.source_detail: Merriam-Webster records breach-of-peace and public-order uses, including public disorder.

facts.statement: can mean an abnormal physical or mental condition
facts.source_detail: Merriam-Webster records an abnormal physical or mental condition; this is the medical noun family.

facts.statement: the verb can disturb order or normal functions transitively
facts.source_detail: Merriam-Webster lists the transitive verb senses of disturbing order and regular or normal functions.

facts.statement: has a formal noun sense meaning a lack of organization
facts.source_detail: Oxford Learner’s Dictionaries presents disorder as a formal state of being untidy or lacking organization.

facts.statement: the medical noun occurs with have, suffer from, and be diagnosed with
facts.source_detail: Oxford Learner’s Dictionaries gives common medical frames around a disorder and disorders.

facts.statement: can refer to violent or unruly public group behavior
facts.source_detail: Oxford Learner’s Dictionaries distinguishes public violent behavior and official/news usage.

facts.statement: public disorder is an official, news, or formal expression
facts.source_detail: Oxford marks the public-order sense in formal public and official contexts.

facts.statement: common combinations include public disorder, civil disorder, and violent disorder
facts.source_detail: Oxford and Collins entries give public-order compounds and collocations in this sense family.

facts.statement: the rare verb can disarrange or throw something into disorder
facts.source_detail: Collins records the transitive verb meaning to disarrange or disturb the arrangement of something.

facts.statement: the verb can disturb health or normal functions in formal usage
facts.source_detail: Collins records the transitive verb extension to disturb health or normal functions.

facts.statement: is formed from dis- and order and is associated with a departure from order
facts.source_detail: Oxford and Collins give the dis- plus order formation and late-medieval history.

facts.statement: disorderly is a directly related adjective
facts.source_detail: Collins records disorderly as the adjective meaning lacking order or disturbing public order.

facts.statement: disordered is a participial adjective related to disorder
facts.source_detail: The dictionaries support the regular past-participle form and adjective use in disordered arrangements or functions.

facts.statement: has second-syllable stress in the standard US and UK pronunciations
facts.source_detail: Cambridge pronunciation provides the US /dɪsˈɔːrdər/ and UK /dɪsˈɔːdə/ transcriptions.
